Empirical Research Plan: Massachusetts Health‐Insurance Reform, 2004–2009
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) supplemented with a staggered-event-study and (as a robustness exercise) a synthetic-control estimate of aggregate coverage.

Why DID?  
• The reform was a discrete, state-level policy shock that applied to (almost) every resident of Massachusetts but not to residents of other states.  
• We observe long panels of repeated cross-sections before and after the shock for MA and many potential control states.  
• Outcomes are measured quarterly (NIS) or annually (CPS/BRFSS), giving sufficient pre- and post-periods to test for pre-trends and to estimate dynamic treatment effects.  
• Because treatment is at the state level, IV or RDD are not natural fits; RDD would require a running variable with a discontinuous cutoff, which we do not have.  
• A generalized event-study (Sun & Abraham 2021) deals with staggered implementation of Medicaid expansions (tiny timing differences across counties inside MA) and the phase-in of the mandate, while the main “on/off” DID is easily interpretable.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Treated unit: Discharges/residents in Massachusetts.  
• Treated = 1 for observations in Massachusetts in quarters ≥ 2007Q3 (date when the individual mandate became enforceable and the great majority of expansions were in place).  
  – In robustness we will code treatment to begin 2006Q2 (law passage) and 2006Q4 (first CommCare enrollments) to test sensitivity to timing.

Control group  
• Primary control: Discharges/residents in the 41 HCUP-participating states that did not enact broad coverage reforms during 2004–2009 (drop Vermont, Maine, Hawaii, etc. that had contemporaneous Medicaid expansions)  
• Secondary controls:  
  – (i) New England comparison states (CT, RI, NH) only;  
  – (ii) Synthetic control of donor states chosen to best match MA on pre-reform outcome means and trends;  
  – (iii) Weighting each control state by inverse variance / population to avoid dominance of large states.

Treatment timing  
• Baseline: Post = 1 from 2007Q3 forward.  
• Event-study coefficients for leads (t = −8 … −1 quarters) and lags (t = 0 … +9 quarters) relative to 2007Q3.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Parallel-Trends: In the absence of Chapter 58, MA outcomes would have evolved like outcomes in the control states.  
– Plausibility: Pre-reform growth rates in uninsurance, hospital utilization, and quality indicators look visually similar; we will test formal pre-trend equality.  
A2. No Spillovers: The reform affected only MA residents and MA hospitals.  
– Plausibility: Some cross-state patient flows exist but represent <5 % of MA hospital discharges; we will drop non-MA residents treated in MA hospitals and check robustness to excluding border-county hospitals.  
A3. Stable Composition: Hospital and survey sampling frames stay comparable over time.  
– Plausibility: NIS sampling weights are explicitly designed for consistency; we will confirm by checking distribution of hospital characteristics over time.  
A4. No Concurrent Policies Differentially Affecting MA: There were no other MA-specific shocks in 2007 that drive outcomes.  
– Plausibility: The 2007–2009 recession hit all states; including state-specific linear trends and unemployment controls mitigates this concern.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
-----------------------------------------
T1. Differential Great-Recession Effects  
• Massachusetts’ labor market was somewhat less affected.  
• Mitigation: Include quarterly state unemployment rates and industry-mix controls; allow state-specific linear (or quadratic) time trends.

T2. Coding or Reporting Changes in NIS  
• If MA hospitals improved documentation in 2007 (e.g., because of pay-for-performance rules), observed patient-safety indicators could mechanically change.  
• Mitigation: Examine “hard” utilization outcomes (length of stay, ER admission source) separately; conduct falsification tests on coding-insensitive outcomes (e.g., appendicitis admissions).

T3. Patient Migration / Border Shopping  
• Uninsured NH residents may cross into MA post-reform.  
• Mitigation: (i) Drop non-MA residents; (ii) Run specification using patient ZIP state; (iii) Border-county difference-in-discontinuities comparing close-distance hospitals.

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional fixed effects
library(did)          # Callaway-Sant’Anna DID/event study
library(ggplot2)
library(Synth)        # synthetic control robustness

# 1. Load Data -------------------------------------------------------------
nis  <- fread("nis_quarterly_2004_2009.csv")   # hospital discharge level
cps  <- fread("cps_state_coverage_2004_2009.csv")  # state-year insurance
brf  <- fread("brfss_preventive_2004_2009.csv")    # state-year behaviors

# 2. Variable Construction -------------------------------------------------
nis[, post  := (year > 2007 | (year==2007 & quarter>=3))]
nis[, treat := (state_fips == "25")]             # 25 = Massachusetts
nis[, treat_post := post*treat]

# Aggregate to state-quarter so variance is manageable
nis_sq <- nis[, .(
  los_mean    = weighted.mean(length_of_stay, discharge_weight),
  er_share    = weighted.mean(adm_via_er==1, discharge_weight),
  uninsured   = weighted.mean(payer=="UNINSURED", discharge_weight),
  medicaid    = weighted.mean(payer=="MEDICAID", discharge_weight),
  total_disc  = sum(discharge_weight)
), by = .(state_fips, year, quarter, post, treat)]

# 3. Main DID Regression ---------------------------------------------------
# Example outcome: uninsured share among discharges
did_main <- feols(uninsured ~ treat*post + 
                    state_unemp_rate +                 # macro control
                    year_quarter | 
                    state_fips +                       # state FE
                    year_quarter,                      # time FE
                  weights = ~total_disc,
                  data = nis_sq)

etable(did_main, dict = c("treat:post"="MA Post"))

# 4. Event-Study (Abraham & Sun) ------------------------------------------
nis_sq[, rel_time := (year - 2007)*4 + (quarter - 3)]
es_res <- att_gt(yname = "uninsured", tname = "rel_time",
                 idname = "state_fips", gname = "treat",
                 xformla = ~ state_unemp_rate,
                 data = nis_sq, panel = FALSE)

ggdid(es_res)

# 5. Heterogeneity Example: age groups ------------------------------------
# age_grp already in NIS; loop over groups
out_list <- lapply(unique(nis_sq$age_grp), function(a){
  feols(uninsured ~ treat*post | state_fips + year_quarter,
        data = nis_sq[age_grp==a]) })
etable(out_list)

# 6. Robustness: Synthetic Control ----------------------------------------
ma_cov <- cps[state=="MA", .(year, uninsured)]
donor  <- cps[state!="MA" & good_control==1]
dat_synth <- dataprep(
  foo = cps,
  predictors = c("median_income", "poverty_rate", "hospital_beds"),
  dependent = "uninsured",
  unit.variable = "state_id",
  time.variable = "year",
  special.predictors = list(),
  treatment.identifier = 25,
  controls.identifier = donor$state_id,
  time.predictors.prior = 2004:2006,
  time.optimize.ssr = 2004:2006,
  time.plot = 2004:2009)
scm <- synth(dat_synth)
path.plot(synth.res = scm, dataprep.res = dat_synth)

```

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Theory predicts:  
• Uninsurance in MA should fall sharply (-6 to ‑7 pp among adults 18-64, roughly matching pre-ACA estimates).  
• Insurance mix: big rise in Medicaid & private nongroup (Connector) coverage; tiny fall in employer-sponsored insurance (crowd-out 1–2 pp).  
• Hospital utilization: possibly more outpatient/preventive care and slightly shorter inpatient stays (better management), but ER share could fall only modestly (evidence from Oregon). Expect −5 % ER admissions per capita.  
• Patient-safety indicators should improve (↓ 10 % in PSIs for preventable complications).  
• Costs: hospital-specific cost-to-charge ratios may not move much; total charges per discharge fall 2–3 %.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
-------------------------------------------
C1 Parallel pre-trends verified visually/statistically: 1  
C2 No anticipation of treatment: 1  
C3 Stable composition of treated & control groups over time: 0.5 (some recession effects)  
C4 No spillovers or interference: 0.5 (border spillovers possible)  
C5 Treatment sharply defined & correctly measured: 1  

Total: 4 / 5 – overall credible but not bullet-proof.

End of Plan
